A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 292-paper causal-graph benchmark, renamed from ReCAST to ReCITE. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison; reporting inconsistencies are document issues rather than missing evidence.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of five LLMs, node-name ablations, annotation agreement, performance analyses, and model and human case studies.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of ten LLMs and additional judge-agreement, alternative-scoring, graph-topology, textual-diversity, and error analyses.

M1.justification: The benchmark-building pipeline, graph-generation and name-assisted prompts, and primary fine-grained judging rubric and scoring rules are substantively retained. The rename, additional backend disclosures, and supplementary evaluation variants do not establish a new causal-graph inference method.

E1.justification: The core 292-paper graph-construction task is retained; replacing economics-oriented domain labels with 17 OpenAlex fields does not establish expanded benchmark membership. Appendix F adds 250 economics and 248 non-economics reference papers for comparative embedding analysis, extending the data used in supporting analyses.

E2.justification: The main, name-assisted, and TEA-GLM comparisons add Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro and Flash, GLM 4.7, and Kimi K2, while removing o3-mini as an evaluated comparator. The cutoff comparison replaces o3-mini with R1 and Qwen. Llama remains in the main tables but is omitted from v3's explicitness heatmaps.

E3.justification: v3 adds graph-only binary scoring without importance weights and matched cross-judge evaluation on 41 outputs. Domain analysis changes from R1-assigned categories to OpenAlex classifications and embedding clusters, while the cutoff analysis adopts model-specific dates. The explicitness heatmaps also report different binning, although their labels and accompanying prose are inconsistent.

E4.justification: Appendices C–G and O add judge agreement and family-bias checks, scoring robustness, topology and cyclicity analyses, embedding-based diversity and clustering, quantitative reasoning-length analysis, and aggregate error breakdowns. The earlier node-name ablation, TEA-GLM comparison, and human/base-model case studies are retained or expanded, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 already reports standard deviations, annotation agreement, and Mann–Whitney cutoff tests. v3 substantially expands statistical analysis with judge correlations and calibration differences, scoring-rank correlations, topology and reasoning-length significance tests, and ANOVA/Kruskal–Wallis tests with effect-size reporting. Detailed cutoff p-values disappear; neither version establishes repeated-seed reproducibility.

E6.justification: The reported leader changes from R1 at 0.477 F1 in v2 Table 2 to Claude Opus 4.5 at 0.535 in v3 Table 3; R1's reported score becomes 0.460. Numerous new model and analysis results are added, including unweighted edge F1 scores of 0.111–0.297. These are updated evaluations, not demonstrated same-setting gains. Annotation prose is revised to 879 edges and 674 nodes, matching the existing per-graph table totals.

T1.justification: The explicitness equations are complementary re-expressions of the two existing confounding measures, with their main-text and appendix roles exchanged. Added precision, recall, and SHD formulas document empirical scoring; no substantive new theory, formal assumptions, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a first realistic benchmark for causal-graph construction from academic text, introduce automated graph judging, and identify causal reasoning as the main bottleneck despite providing node names. The expanded model set and revised headline F1 update the supporting evidence without materially redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations about judge bias, graph topology, semantic diversity, and directionality versus graph-recovery errors, and expands the justification for specifying node counts. Its new limitations address English-only coverage, zero-shot evaluation, text genres, system-dynamics graphs, and LLM-based judging. Some interpretations conflict with their supporting displays, notably explicitness trends and calibration differences.

D1.justification: v3 newly identifies DeepSeek v3.2 as the primary judge, specifies 20 Qwen context-length exclusions, adds GPT-5-mini as a formatting backend, and documents embedding procedures. It identifies 20 undergraduate annotators, their incentives and estimated effort, and supplies an annotation-form screenshot. Repository access information is added, although a footnote still defers the full dataset release until publication; total experimental cost changes from under $250 to under $1000.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A substantially broaden positioning against prior benchmarks, adding CausalTalk, CaLM, CausalProbe-2024, CausalGraphBench, and Lee et al., among other references. New discussions distinguish their inputs and task requirements from full-document graph construction and expand grounding in causal cognition, document extraction, and LLM judging.

P1.justification: v3 extensively revises the introduction, benchmark framing, evaluation explanation, and conclusion, and replaces ReCAST/confounding terminology with ReCITE/explicitness. It integrates the formerly separate technical appendix into lettered sections, consolidates references, relocates analyses and scoring documentation, and adds limitations and ethics sections.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the introductory example, explicitness heatmaps, domain radar chart, and model case-study graph. It adds topology, embedding, reasoning-length, and annotation-form figures plus many analysis tables, while replacing earlier domain-count and journal-distribution displays. Typography, table sizing, prompt pagination, and overall layout are also substantially revised.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v2's limited judge validation through additional comparisons and scoring checks, and improves annotation transparency and limitations. However, Figure 2's displayed trend conflicts with its explicitness interpretation, Tables 8–9 contain inconsistent calibration differences or signs, and Appendix F's MMD interpretation conflicts with its stated distances. These problems affect central validation and difficulty claims, leaving the net quality benefit uncertain despite the substantial additions.
